title: Messages, phone calls and invitations
goal: Write natural WhatsApp messages, make polite phone calls, and read a Sundanese invitation without getting lost.
bekal: how to open and close a written message in Sundanese
abbreviations Sundanese speakers use on WhatsApp
reading a celebration invitation and its set phrases

dialogs.title: Paguneman — Calling Kang Yayan
dialogs.intro: Rani needs to ask about a file she left at the office. She calls her colleague, and the whole rhythm of a Sundanese phone call plays out here.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.id: Waalaikumsalam. Excuse me, Kang, it's Rani.

lines.speaker: Kang Yayan:
lines.text: Oh Téh Rani. Kumaha, aya naon?
lines.literal: oh Téh Rani. how, there-is what?

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Punten ngaganggu wengi-wengi. Nuju sibuk teu?
lines.id: Sorry to bother you so late. Are you busy?

lines.speaker: Kang Yayan:
lines.text: Henteu, mangga waé. Aya naon, Téh?
lines.id: No, go ahead. What is it?
lines.literal: no, please just. there-is what, Téh?

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Berkas laporan téh kantun di méja abdi henteu?
lines.id: Did I leave that report file on my desk?
lines.literal: file report [téh] left-behind at desk my not?

lines.speaker: Kang Yayan:
lines.text: Sakedap, abdi tingali heula… Muhun, aya di dieu.
lines.id: Hang on, let me look… Yes, it's here.
lines.literal: moment, I look first… yes, there-is at here.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.id: Thank goodness. Could you take a photo of it, Kang?

lines.speaker: Kang Yayan:
lines.text: Tangtos. Engké abdi kirimkeun ka WA.
lines.id: Sure. I'll send it to you on WhatsApp.
lines.literal: certainly. later I send to WA.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Hatur nuhun pisan, Kang. Punten ngarepotkeun.
lines.id: Thank you so much, Kang. Sorry for the trouble.
lines.literal: thank you very, Kang. excuse-me troubling.

lines.speaker: Kang Yayan:
lines.id: You're welcome. It's fine, no trouble at all.
lines.literal: same-same. no what-what just, not troubling.

notes: **Kantun** has two common meanings: **left behind** (as here) and **left over, remaining** (*kantun dua* = only two left). The loma forms are **tinggaleun** and **kari**.
**Wios** = it's fine, no problem (lemes); loma: **teu nanaon**. It's very common in phone calls and texts, often written *wios waé* or just *wios*.

**Dipotokeun** comes from *poto* (photo) + *di-…-keun* = to have a photo taken of it. Notice how easily loanwords slot into Sundanese affixes: *di-WA-keun* (sent by WhatsApp), *dichat-keun*, *diprint-keun* are all normal office talk.
**Nuju sibuk teu?** (are you busy?) is an almost mandatory way to open a call. Calling and getting straight to the point without asking feels rushed.
**Punten ngaganggu wengi-wengi**: apologizing for the time of the call. Its morning partner is *punten ngaganggu énjing-énjing*. It's a formality that's always appreciated.

In West Java, phone calls almost always open and close with **assalamualaikum**, even for work. If the person you're talking to isn't Muslim, *wilujeng énjing/wengi* (good morning/evening) and *hatur nuhun* are enough.

grammars.title: Written Sundanese on screen
body: WhatsApp messages in Sundanese have their own habits, and knowing them lets you read what comes in. What surprises newcomers most: the accent on *é* nearly always disappears, and lots of words get shortened.
after: ⚠️ Because the accent on *é* disappears, words like *sae*, *bade*, *tehna* have to be read from context. That's exactly the skill you practiced in Unit 2, and this is where it pays off.
A polite Sundanese message almost always opens with **punten** and closes with **hatur nuhun**. A message without them feels hurried, even if the content is fine.

For formal messages (to a boss, a teacher or an older person) the order is fixed: **greeting, punten, introduce yourself, your message, hatur nuhun, greeting**. Skipping the self-introduction is the most common newcomer mistake, since your number may not be saved in their phone.

blocks.title: On the phone
items: **Punten, ieu sareng saha?** — Excuse me, who am I speaking to?
**Sakedap nya, abdi tingali heula.** — Hang on, let me have a look.
**Sorana teu kadangu.** — I can't hear you.
**Tiasa diulang deui?** — Could you say that again?
**Engké abdi telepon deui.** — I'll call you back later.

blocks.text: A polite written message to a boss, in full:

blocks.title: Sample message
items: *Badé ngawartosan, laporan kanggo rapat énjing parantos rengse. Filena tos dikirim ka email Bapa.*
*Upami aya nu kedah dirévisi, mangga wartosan waé.*

blocks.text: Celebration invitations in West Java are often written in high lemes Sundanese, with words that differ from everyday speech. These lines turn up almost every time:

head: Invitation line
English
rows: In the name of God, the Most Merciful
By the grace of God, the Most Holy
On the occasion of the marriage of our son/daughter
Your presence would be a great joy to us

blocks.text: ⚠️ **Simkuring** (or *sim kuring*) is the humblest form of "I/we," used in formal writing and speeches. You don't need it in conversation, but you'll read it on every invitation.

blocks.title: Replying to an invitation
items: **Insya Allah abdi ngiring sumping.** — God willing, I'll be there.
**Ngiring bingah kana rencangna.** — I share in your joy.
**Hapunten abdi teu tiasa ngaluuhan.** — Sorry, I'm unable to attend.
**Mugia acarana lancar sareng barokah.** — May the event go smoothly and be blessed.
**Wilujeng, mugia janten kulawarga sakinah.** — Congratulations, may you have a happy, peaceful family.
**Titip amplop waé nya, punten teu tiasa sumping.** — I'll send an envelope, sorry I can't come.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right phone phrase.
items: Asking if the other person is busy: ____

exercises.prompt: What's the full form or meaning of these message abbreviations?
Translate these invitation lines into English.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: Halo, assalamualaikum. — Punten, ieu sareng saha? — Nuju sibuk teu? — Punten ngaganggu. — Sakedap nya, abdi tingali heula. — Hatur nuhun, assalamualaikum.
parantos (already) — it's fine — hatur nuhun (thank you) — kumaha (how) — saé (good) — teu acan (not yet)

We kindly request your presence. — On the occasion of our son's marriage. — Your presence would be a great joy. — Thank you for your attention. — God willing, I'll be there. — May the event go smoothly and be blessed.
Nuju sibuk teu? — Sakedap nya, abdi tingali heula. — Engké abdi kirimkeun ka WA. — Punten ngarepotkeun, hatur nuhun. — Insya Allah abdi ngiring sumping.
